summary:
Rwanda does not criminalise same-sex intimacy, and the age of consent is 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. A trans visitor therefore faces no statute aimed at identity or consensual relationships. That baseline does not describe what happens on the street. A 2025 submission by the Human Rights First Rwanda Association to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuse directed at transgender people: harassment during identity checks and arbitrary arrests on vagrancy and public-order grounds, including during periodic round-ups in Kigali.

The detention record extends beyond that submission. In November 2020 Vice reported violent detentions of transgender people in Rwanda, describing how on Christmas Day 2018 a singer known as Bella, booked to perform at a hotel in Kigali, was stopped by police officers on the street after her show; her name was changed in the account over safety concerns. A 2016 United States State Department country report separately records LGBTQ Rwandans being harassed, blackmailed and arrested by police under public-order and morality laws, and LGBTI rights groups reporting occasional harassment by neighbours and police.

Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no domestic legal gender recognition path exists for a trans person. Article 26 of the Constitution, adopted in May 2003, recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman; same-sex marriages, civil unions and equivalent unions are not recognised, so a foreign trans marriage is not given effect under the constitutional text as reported.

Entry and protection machinery runs in the opposite direction to the street record. In 2024 the government issued immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. The 2024 Asylum and Humanitarian Protection Decision Making Standard Operating Procedures require interviews to be conducted so the applicant can present the grounds of the application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The 2014 Manual on Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures imposes a comparable requirement at appeal hearings.

Healthcare access is protected on paper. The Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy issued by the Ministry of Health in 2018 states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief or disability are equally entitled to receive health services, and applies across public, private and NGO sectors. Against that, there is no general anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity: Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution do not list either ground, with Article 16 naming ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability and others.
